summary:
This intelligent mission-control and autonomous navigation platform, developed by Team UniSPARK, enables safe, data-driven exploration on the Martian surface. Designed to overcome extreme hazards and deep-space communication delays, it serves as a real-time tactical assistant for astronauts and rovers.

Architecture:
Engineered with a decoupled architecture, the system combines a robust .NET 9 Backend API with a responsive React Command HUD. The backend processes spatial grid data, obstacles, and environmental telemetry—including thermal and radiation levels—to run dynamic pathfinding algorithms. Through RESTful API integration, the frontend renders interactive maps like Jezero Crater, heatmaps, and live logs, allowing operators to inspect coordinates instantly.

Key Impact:

Multi-Route Optimization: Computes and contrasts three trajectories in real time: the Shortest Route for efficiency, the Safest Route to bypass radiation spikes and cliffs, and an Emergency Route for critical missions.

Hazard Mitigation: Visualizes thermal and radiation layers directly over the terrain grid, helping crews anticipate deadly shifts.

Decision Support: Eliminates the 4-to-24-minute Earth-Mars communication bottleneck by empowering crews with immediate spatial intelligence, maximizing survivability.
details:
1. What It Does & How It Works

Developed by Team UniSPARK, this project is an autonomous Martian surface navigation and tactical mission-control platform designed to guide astronauts and planetary rovers safely across hazardous terrain (such as Jezero Crater).

The system operates on a decoupled, real-time client-server architecture:

  • Spatial & Environmental Processing: The backend ingests multi-layered planetary data—including topographical elevation, surface obstacles, thermal gradients, and ionizing radiation levels—mapping them onto an interactive coordinate grid.
    • The Shortest Route: Optimized purely for minimal distance and energy conservation.
    • The Safest Route: Dynamically penalized against high radiation spikes, extreme cold zones, and steep cliffs to guarantee crew and hardware survival.
    • The Emergency/Aggressive Route: Engineered for time-critical rescue or rapid-response scenarios where speed overrides moderate environmental risk.
  • Interactive Command HUD: Through RESTful API communication, the frontend renders these trajectories in real time, allows operators to toggle between standard, thermal, and radiation heatmap layers, inspects specific sector coordinates with visual reconnaissance previews, and streams live system telemetry logs.

2. Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Overcoming Deep-Space Communication Latency: Earth-Mars communication delays range from 4 to 24 minutes each way, making real-time remote piloting from Earth impossible during emergencies. Our platform empowers local Martian crews and rovers with immediate, autonomous spatial intelligence.
  • Maximizing Mission Survivability: By turning invisible threats like solar/cosmic radiation pockets and sudden thermal drops into clear visual layers, astronauts can make proactive, life-saving navigation decisions before entering danger zones.
  • Operational Efficiency & Scientific Output: Optimizing routes reduces rover battery drain and mechanical wear, allowing missions to cover more geological ground and collect higher-value scientific data per Martian solar day (Sol).

3. Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software Used

To ensure enterprise-grade performance, scalability, and rapid deployment, our team utilized a modern full-stack engineering pipeline:

  • Backend Development: Built using C# and .NET 9 (ASP.NET Core Web API) for high-throughput spatial calculations, RESTful endpoint routing, and pathfinding logic.
  • Frontend Development: Engineered with React.js, JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, and custom CSS3 to create a zero-latency, high-contrast aerospace Command HUD capable of rendering dynamic grid states and data layers smoothly.
  • Development & Testing Environment: Visual Studio 2022 and Visual Studio Code for core development, Postman and Swagger/OpenAPI for API endpoint verification, and Chrome DevTools for frontend performance profiling.
  • Version Control & Deployment: Git and GitHub for collaborative team workflow, paired with cloud hosting platforms (Render/Railway for the .NET API and Vercel/Netlify for the React client).
  • Hardware: Developed and stress-tested on multi-core developer workstations configured to simulate concurrent API requests and real-time telemetry streaming.

4. Creativity & Innovation

  • Context-Aware Multi-Route Decision Matrix: Unlike traditional navigation tools that offer a single "best" path, our system acknowledges that space exploration requires trade-offs. Giving commanders a side-by-side comparison of Safety vs. Speed vs. Efficiency mirrors real-world NASA mission-control decision-making.
  • Unified Tactical HUD Design: Instead of burying astronauts in raw spreadsheets, we merged geospatial mapping, environmental heatmaps, sector imagery, and live terminal logs into a single, intuitive aerospace interface designed for high-stress environments.
  • Resilient Hybrid Simulation Mode: The frontend includes an intelligent fallback architecture—if network connectivity to the central server drops, local pathfinding algorithms seamlessly take over so navigation never fails.

5. Key Factors Considered by Our Team

  • Human & Hardware Safety Thresholds: We factored in how prolonged radiation exposure degrades both human health and sensitive rover electronics, weighting our safest-path algorithm accordingly.
  • Extreme Thermal Fluctuations: Martian temperatures swing drastically between day and night; our thermal layer accounts for micro-climates within craters that could freeze mechanical actuators.
  • System Decoupling & Fault Tolerance: By separating the .NET 9 computational engine from the React visualization layer, the system remains modular, easy to upgrade with real NASA/ESA satellite APIs in the future, and resilient against single-point failures.
  • UI Ergonomics in High-Stress Scenarios: We designed the interface with dark-mode aerospace aesthetics, color-coded risk indicators (Cyan for safe, Amber for target, Crimson for hazards), and instant click-to-inspect workflows to minimize cognitive load on the operator.
